Our Perspective

Rates Eased. Demand Kept Falling.

Mortgage rates came down a little in October, but contracts kept falling, supply kept climbing, and the Cromford Market Index sank deep into buyer territory.

October closed with 5,140 listings sold across Greater Phoenix by Cromford's count, down 12.6% from September and 16.8% below October 2025, the lowest October count since 2007. October had 21 working days against 22 a year ago, and even per working day closings were down about 12.8%. Maricopa County affidavits recorded 5,169 closings, down 14.7% on the year and the lowest October in records going back to 1999, with resales off 13.4% at 4,144 and new homes off 19.4% at 1,025.

The forward gauges kept sliding. On November 1, pending listings were down 11.7% over the month to 3,411 and listings under contract were down 13.1% to 5,705, 19.7% and 22.3% below a year ago. Part of that is the usual dip right after month-end, but on a seven-day average, listings under contract still fell about 10.0% in October, the steepest October decline since 2022. Buyers accepted 5,911 new contracts, down 6.4% from September and 20.1% from October 2025. Meanwhile active listings excluding UCB and CCBS rose 9.6% to 28,107, and the contract ratio fell from 25.60 to 20.30, its lowest level since February 2009.

This was not a rate shock. Mortgage News Daily had the 30-year fixed at 7.30% on November 3, down from 7.57% a month earlier, which Cromford calculates saves about $65 a month on an 80% loan against the typical $444,000 home. By November 9 the MND rate was 7.18%, down 0.30 points over the month but still 0.86 points above a year ago. The easing did not lift contracts. In October, 1,303 listings fell out of contract and went back on the market, 22.0 for every 100 new contracts, compared with 18.5 a year ago.

Pricing is sending two signals, and only one of them describes the typical home. Average price per square foot rose 3.9% to $304.65, but that came largely from the top of the market: closings of $2 million or more rose from 150 to 178, while closings under $1 million fell from 5,331 to 4,581. The median price per square foot slipped 0.9% to $249.68 and the median sales price fell 1.3% to $444,000. Sellers still collected 97.28% of final list price. In Maricopa County, the overall median eased to $470,000, down 1.9% on the year and about 5.4% lower once inflation is counted.

The Cromford Market Index for all areas and types fell below 70 on October 21 for the first time since March 2009, and the concise snapshot had it at 64.6 on November 8, against 78.1 a year ago. In the November 5 large-city table, the average reading was down 14.9% from a month earlier, and for the fifth week running all 18 cities were moving toward buyers over the month, even though Avondale and Queen Creek edged up that week. Only 2 cities remain seller's markets, Scottsdale at 129.8 and Paradise Valley at 112.5, with 5 balanced and 11 buyer's markets, the most since December 2022. Cromford expects the median sales price to stay flat at best, or more likely fall slightly, over the next few months.

Market context
On Cromford's monthly chart, new listings rose 2.08% over the month to 8,979, and active listings climbed 5.57% to 25,575, 9.78% above a year ago. Cromford's first-of-month count of active listings excluding UCB and CCBS reads the same way, up 9.6% to 28,107 on November 1 and 8.3% above a year ago, the biggest October rise since 2023. Two different counts, one conclusion. Days of inventory climbed to 146.3 from 134.6, and by November 8 months of supply excluding UCB had reached 5.6, up from 4.5 a month earlier and 4.1 a year ago. Expired and cancelled listings rose in the East Valley to 650 from 590, and in the Northeast Valley to 342 from 287. Cromford's read is that this is not a flood of new listings; supply is building because too few homes are going under contract, so pricing to the market from day one matters more now than it has all year.

Market intelligence

4 Facts You Need To Consider

01

The contract pipeline is the thinnest in years. On November 1, pending listings stood at 3,411 and listings under contract at 5,705, down 19.7% and 22.3% from a year ago, and the contract ratio fell to 20.30, the lowest since February 2009. Part of that is the usual dip right after month-end.

02

Notices of Trustee Sale reached 518 in October, the most in a single month since April 2019, with 4,891 filed from January through October, up 13.9% and the highest for those months since 2018. Completed Trustee's Deeds rose 47% to 1,318.

03

New home closings fell again, to 1,025 from 1,109 in September, down 19.4% on the year and the lowest October since 2015. Their share of the Maricopa market still rose to 19.8%, the highest of 2026, because resales fell slightly faster month over month (−8.3% vs. −7.6%).

04

The average went up. The typical home did not. Average price per square foot rose 4.0% from $293.21 on October 1 to $305.01 on November 1, while the median slipped 0.7% from $251.88 to $250.12, the widest one-month split since at least 2011. Take out closings of $2 million or more and the average rose by only about 60 cents.

What The Heck Is Going On

October was the month weak demand showed up in closings. Cromford's first-of-month count put closed listings at 5,140, down 16.8% on the year, and monthly dollar volume fell 13.0% to $3,201 million, a smaller drop than closings because more expensive homes closed. Excluding the Sedona and Verde Valley listings that joined ARMLS, closings were down 17.0% rather than 16.8%. The listing success rate on that count fell from 68.6% to 62.9%, the lowest October reading since 2010, so more sellers gave up during the month.

Rates eased a little. It didn't bring buyers back. Mortgage News Daily had the 30-year fixed at 7.30% on November 3 and 7.18% on November 9, below its 52-week high of 7.61% but still well above the 6.32% of a year ago. The Cromford monthly chart, a separate series, shows the same squeeze: listings under contract at 5,350, down 20.36% from a year ago, and sold homes at 4,609, down 17.84%. With supply this high and contracts this low, Cromford expects fewer closings in November and December than a year ago.

Pricing is splitting by price point. On the same monthly chart, average price per square foot rose 3.95% over the month to $304.08, while the median slipped to $249.42 from $251.35 a month earlier and $253.92 a year ago. Case-Shiller showed Phoenix down 0.53% for the month and up 0.42% on the year, but that index covers sales from June to August 2026, before the latest slide. Cromford expects the median price to hold flat at best or slip slightly; a rising average reflects more luxury closings, not appreciation.

Seller Reality Check

Buyers Hold The Leverage.

Across Greater Phoenix, supply is building faster than buyers can absorb it. Months of supply excluding UCB reached 5.6 on November 8, against 4.5 a month earlier and 4.1 a year ago. Cromford's monthly listing success rate was 64.3% for October and 62.1% through November 7. Concessions remain the norm: 56.8% of October closings (2,618 of 4,609) included seller-paid concessions at a median of $10,532, down from 57.9% in September, and 54.3% month to date.

The November 5 CMI table shows how uneven this is across the valley. Only Scottsdale at 129.8 and Paradise Valley at 112.5 are still seller's markets among the 18 large cities. Chandler has left seller territory at 106.2, Phoenix is balanced at 91.5, and Gilbert slipped to 89.4, just into a buyer's market. The West Valley is further toward buyers, with Peoria at 66.3, Goodyear at 56.7, Surprise at 55.9, and Buckeye at 42.9. Southeast of the valley, San Tan Valley at 45.9, Queen Creek at 44.0, and Maricopa at 40.8 sit deep in buyer's territory. Among the smaller cities, only Anthem and Sun Lakes are still seller's markets, while Sun City West has dropped to balanced.

Pricing depends on where you are. On November 1, single-family listings under contract were below a year ago in every price band from $300K to $1.5M, by as much as 35.7% between $700K and $800K. Luxury neighborhoods within 10 miles of downtown Phoenix were up a typical 9% over the past year, while those beyond 20 miles fell about 1%. Cromford expects more choice and room to negotiate in the coming weeks, especially in the Southeast and West Valley. 2026 resales spent a median of only 14 days at their final list price, and homes cut five or more times still sold for 98.3% of the final price but just 86.5% of the first. Overpricing does not earn a better offer. It postpones the sale.

Full-service representation, negotiation expertise, and market intelligence that flat-fee models cannot replicate. With only 2 of 18 large cities still seller's markets and all 18 moving toward buyers for a fifth week, the right advocate is not a line item: it is the outcome.

Closings vs. Active Listings

Promising more to win the listing isn't the same as selling it. In October, KW Sonoran Living closed 54 homes against 119 active listings, about 45 per 100. Flat Fee / Other closed 18 against 146, about 12, and Homie closed none of its 7. A low fee doesn't help much if the home doesn't sell.

Economic Development

Capital Keeps Landing.

CRE DailyRead story ↗

TSMC Phoenix Campus Fuels a $265B Suburban Property Boom

TSMC’s $265 billion Arizona investment — the largest foreign greenfield project in U.S. history — is reshaping the Northwest Valley. Industrial vacancy there fell from 16% to 8% (Colliers, June), Taiwanese investors have put in about $500 million since 2021 (GPEC), and Taicoon paid $88 million for land near the campus for a planned $1 billion mixed-use project. TSMC has hired about 3,500 people in Arizona and plans about 2,500 more, with Fab 2 complete and volume production targeted for 3Q 2027, slightly ahead of schedule.

ABC15Read story ↗

Chandler data center campus enters next growth phase with large users in tow

Aligned Data Centers Continuum Propco is expanding along Chandler’s Price Road Corridor between Germann and Queen Creek, with public Maricopa County records naming Google as a tenant and Oracle as a customer (ABC15 / Phoenix Business Journal, Oct. 19). Two planned facilities total roughly 400 MW of capacity. Aligned was acquired this summer in a deal valuing the company at about $40 billion.

Hotel BusinessRead story ↗

Plaza Cos., Fayth Hospitality to break ground on dual-branded Hotel Six Four, Mayo Blvd

Plaza Companies and Fayth Hospitality are breaking ground on Hotel Six Four, a 257-room, six-story dual-brand Hilton (133-key Tapestry Collection and 124-key Homewood Suites) at 64th Street and Mayo Boulevard in North Phoenix. JLL arranged a $70.85 million construction loan. The site sits less than a mile from Mayo Clinic’s Phoenix campus, with an expected 2028 opening.

Market context
The 30-year fixed at Mortgage News Daily was 7.18% on November 9, down 0.09 points on the week and 0.30 points on the month, and 0.86 points above a year ago (6.32%). That is below the 7.45% in last month’s report (October 14) and under the 52-week high of 7.61%, with the 52-week range 5.99% to 7.61%. The rest of the board followed, with the 15-year at 6.83%, FHA at 6.82% and VA at 6.83%. Mortgage News Daily’s headline read “Mortgage Rates Hold Steady at Lows Despite Stronger Jobs Report,” though at 7.18% the 30-year sits closer to its 52-week high than its low. The 10-year Treasury was 4.875%.
